'''Steven Weinberg''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|w|aɪ|n|b|ɜr|ɡ}}; May 3, 1933 – July 23, 2021)<ref name=NYTObit>{{cite news| title= Steven Weinberg, Groundbreaking Nobelist in Physics, Dies at 88| last= McClain| first= Dylan Loeb| work= [[The New York Times]]| url= https://www.nytimes.com/2021/07/25/science/steven-weinberg-groundbreaking-nobelist-in-physics-dies-at-88.html}}</ref> was an American [[Theoretical physics|theoretical physicist]]. He was one of the main developers of the [[Standard Model|standard model of particle physics]].

Weinberg held the Josey Regental Chair in Science at the [[University of Texas at Austin]]. His research on [[elementary particle]]s and [[physical cosmology]] was honored with numerous prizes and awards. He shared the 1979 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] with [[Abdus Salam]] and [[Sheldon Glashow]] for their contributions to the theory of the unified weak and electromagnetic interaction between elementary particles.<ref name= "Nobel Prize">{{cite web |title= The Nobel Prize in Physics 1979 |publisher= [[Nobel Foundation]] |url= http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/1979/index.html |access-date= 9 October 2008 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20090226040152/http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/1979/index.html |archive-date= 26 February 2009 |url-status= live }}</ref>

Weinberg also had an extensive career as a writer. His first textbook was ''Gravitation and Cosmology'' (1972). His three-volume series ''The Quantum Theory of Fields'' is considered a classic. He also wrote [[popular science]], beginning with ''[[The First Three Minutes]]''.<ref name=Pop/> He occasionally wrote articles on various subjects for ''[[The New York Review of Books]]'' and other periodicals.

==Early life==
Steven Weinberg was born on May 3, 1933, in New York City. His parents were [[Jewish]]; his father, Frederick, worked as a court stenographer, while his mother, Eva (née Israel), was a housewife who had immigrated from Germany.<ref>{{cite news|title=Three Scientists, Two Jewish and One Moslem, Win Nobel Prize| url=https://www.jta.org/1979/10/16/archive/three-scientists-two-jewish-and-one-moslem-win-nobel-prize| work=[[Jewish Telegraphic Agency]] | date=October 16, 1979}}</ref><ref name=aso>{{cite web |url=http://www.pbs.org/wgbh/aso/databank/entries/bpwein.html|title=Steven Weinberg 1933– |publisher=[[PBS]] |date=1998}}</ref><ref name=NYTObit/><ref name=nobelbio>{{Cite web |title=Steven Weinberg – Biographical |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/1979/weinberg-bio.html |website=nobelprize.org |access-date=January 25, 2016 }}</ref> 

In a posthumously published memoir, Weinberg wrote: "Whatever native intelligence and intellectual curiosity I may have, I owe to my parents, in particular, my father."<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Farmelo |first=Graham |date=2025-01-27 | author-link=Graham Farmelo |title=How a boy from the Bronx unearthed the workings of the Universe |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-025-00218-9 |journal= Nature |language=en |volume=637 |issue=8048 |pages=1041–1043 |doi=10.1038/d41586-025-00218-9 |pmid=39870789 |bibcode=2025Natur.637.1041F |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2025|p=1}}</ref>

Weinberg first became interested in physics after inheriting a chemistry set from a cousin. His interest in chemistry led him to want to learn about quantum mechanics.<ref name=nobel-interview>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lH28kUzjI5E|title=Steven Weinberg, Nobel Prize in Physics 1979: Interview|access-date=14 October 2026}}</ref>
He found inspiration in [[popular science]], particularly [[George Gamow]] and [[James Jeans]]. He graduated from [[Bronx High School of Science]] in 1950. In the same graduating class was [[Sheldon Glashow]], whose research, independent of Weinberg's, resulted in their sharing the 1979 Nobel in physics with [[Abdus Salam]].<ref name=aip>{{cite web |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210804165727/https://history.aip.org/phn/11503008.html|archive-date=2021-08-04|url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11503008.html| title=Steven Weinberg |publisher=[[American Institute of Physics]] |access-date=July 26, 2021}}</ref><ref name=aso/> Weinberg, Glashow, and [[Gerald Feinberg]] were friends at the school,<ref name=glashowobit/> and Weinberg initially shared an apartment with Glashow when he started at [[Cornell University]], but moved out due to Glashow's "devil-may-care irresponsibility".<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2025|p=10}}</ref>

In 1954, Weinberg received his bachelor's degree from Cornell University, where he majored in [[physics]]. There he resided at the [[Telluride House]].<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2025|pp=10-17}}</ref><ref name=glashowobit/> 

He started graduate studies at the [[Niels Bohr Institute]] in Copenhagen. After a year, Weinberg moved to [[Princeton University]], where he earned his Ph.D. in physics in 1957, completing his dissertation, ''The Role of Strong Interactions in Decay Processes'', under the supervision of [[Sam Treiman]].<ref name=mathgene>{{MathGenealogy|id=105655}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://catalog.princeton.edu/catalog/2844622|title=The role of strong interactions in decay processes|first=Steven|last=Weinberg|date=June 16, 1957|via=catalog.princeton.edu}}</ref><ref name=preskillobit>{{cite journal |last1=Preskill |first1=John |author1-link=John Preskill |title=Steven Weinberg (1933–2021) |journal=Science |department=Retrospective |date=September 3, 2021 |volume=373 |issue=6559 |pages=1092 |doi=10.1126/science.abl8187|pmid=34516845 |bibcode=2021Sci...373.1092P |s2cid=237506142 |doi-access=free }}</ref> He chose to complete his PhD very quickly after his wife grew bored in Princeton and moved back to New York, leaving him alone.<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2025|p=31}}</ref>

==Career and research==
After completing his Ph.D., Weinberg worked as a [[postdoctoral researcher]] at [[Columbia University]] from 1957 to 1959 and then at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. He was promoted to faculty at Berkeley in 1960. Weinberg researched the high-energy behavior of [[quantum field theory]], [[symmetry breaking]], [[pion]] scattering, infrared photons and [[quantum gravity]].<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://cerncourier.com/a/from-bcs-to-the-lhc/|title=From BCS to the LHC |last=Weinberg|first=Steven|author-link=Steven Weinberg| journal= [[CERN Courier]]|date=January 21, 2008|access-date=28 October 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Weinberg, S.|journal=Phys. Rev.|volume=118|pages=838–849|year=1960|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.118.838|title=High-Energy Behavior in Quantum Field Theory|issue=3|bibcode=1960PhRv..118..838W }}; {{cite journal|author=Weinberg, S.|journal=Phys. Rev.|volume=127|pages=965–970|year=1962|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.127.965|title=Broken Symmetries|last2=Salam|first2=Abdus|last3=Weinberg|first3=Steven|issue=3|bibcode=1962PhRv..127..965G }}; {{cite journal|author=Weinberg, S.|journal=Phys. Rev. Lett.|volume=17|pages=616–621|year=1966|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.17.616|title=Pion Scattering Lengths|issue=11|bibcode=1966PhRvL..17..616W }}; {{cite journal|author=Weinberg, S.|journal=Phys. Rev.|volume=140|pages=B516–B524|year=1965|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.140.B516|title=Infrared Photons and Gravitons|issue=2B|bibcode=1965PhRv..140..516W }}</ref> During this time he developed the approach to quantum field theory described in his book ''The Quantum Theory of Fields''<ref>{{cite journal|author=Weinberg, S.|journal=Phys. Rev.|volume=133|pages=B1318–B1332|year=1964|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.133.B1318|title=Feynman Rules for Any Spin|issue=5B|bibcode=1964PhRv..133.1318W }}; {{cite journal|author=Weinberg, S.|journal=Phys. Rev.|volume=134|pages=B882–B896|year=1964|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.134.B882|title=Feynman Rules for Any Spin. II. Massless Particles|issue=4B|bibcode=1964PhRv..134..882W }}; {{cite journal|author=Weinberg, S.|journal=Phys. Rev.|volume=181|pages=1893–1899|year=1969|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.181.1893|title=Feynman Rules for Any Spin. III|issue=5|bibcode=1969PhRv..181.1893W }}</ref> and started to write his textbook ''Gravitation and Cosmology'', having taken up an interest in [[general relativity]] after the discovery of [[cosmic microwave background radiation]].<ref name=NYTObit/>

Weinberg collaborated with [[Abdus Salam]] during a stay at [[Imperial College]] in the 1961-1962 academic year.<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2009|p=208}}</ref>

===Electroweak unification===

In 1966, Weinberg left Berkeley and accepted a lecturer position at Harvard. In 1967 he was a visiting professor at MIT, where he proposed his model of unification of electromagnetism and nuclear weak forces (such as those involved in [[beta-decay]] and [[kaon]]-decay),<ref>{{cite journal|author=Weinberg, S.|journal=Phys. Rev. Lett.|volume=19|pages=1264–1266|url=http://astrophysics.fic.uni.lodz.pl/100yrs/pdf/12/066.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120112142352/http://astrophysics.fic.uni.lodz.pl/100yrs/pdf/12/066.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 12, 2012|year=1967|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.19.1264|title=A Model of Leptons|issue=21|bibcode=1967PhRvL..19.1264W}}</ref> with the masses of the force-carriers of the weak part of the interaction explained by [[spontaneous symmetry breaking]]. One of its predictions was the existence of the [[Higgs boson]]. Weinberg's model, now known as the [[Electroweak interaction|electroweak unification]] theory, had the same symmetry structure that Glashow proposed in 1961: both included the then-unknown weak interaction mechanism between [[leptons]] known as [[neutral current]] and mediated by the [[Z boson]]. 

The 1973 experimental discovery of weak neutral currents that implied the [[Z boson]]'s existence was one verification of the electroweak unification.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Haidt|first=Dieter |author-link=Dieter Haidt | date=3 October 2004 |access-date=28 October 2026 |title=The discovery of the weak neutral currents |journal=[[CERN Courier]]|url=https://cerncourier.com/a/the-discovery-of-the-weak-neutral-currents/}}</ref> 
In 1979, after the 1978 discovery of the predicted amount of parity violation due to Z bosons' mixing with electromagnetic interactions,<ref>{{cite conference |author= Charles Y. Prescott |title= Parity violation in inelastic scattering of polarized electrons |url= https://www.slac.stanford.edu/pubs/slacpubs/2000/slac-pub-2218.pdf |doi= 10.1063/1.31766 |journal= AIP Conference Proceedings |volume= 51 |page= 202 |publisher= American Institute of Physics |conference= Sixth Trieste Conference on Particle Physics |location= Trieste, Italy |date= June 30, 1978}}</ref> Weinberg was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics with Glashow and Salam, who had independently proposed a theory of electroweak unification based on spontaneous symmetry breaking.<ref name= NYTObit/><ref name="aip" />

The 1967 paper in which Weinberg presented this theory is one of the most cited works in high-energy physics.<ref>{{cite web| publisher= [[INSPIRE-HEP]]| url= http://inspirehep.net/info/hep/stats/topcites/2015/alltime.html| title= Top Cited Articles of All Time (2015 edition)| access-date= 14 October 2026| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160729090544/http://inspirehep.net/info/hep/stats/topcites/2015/alltime.html| archive-date= 2016-07-29}}</ref> It cited Higgs's name first, and it has been suggested that the paper's popularity is a reason the Higgs boson was named after Higgs rather than other scientists who also suggested the mechanism.<ref>{{cite book| last= Close| first= Frank| author-link= Frank Close| title= The Infinity Puzzle: Quantum Field Theory and the Hunt for an Orderly Universe| date= 2011| page= 393| quote= There is however an unintended consequence for history in the order that Weinberg cited these authors, which by citing Higgs in front of Brout and Englert inadvertently thrust Higgs's name to the forefront in popular credits}}</ref><ref name= glashowobit>{{cite web|last=Glashow | first=Sheldon | title= In Memoriam: Steven Weinberg|doi=10.37282/991819.21.37|url=https://inference-review.com/article/in-memoriam-steven-weinberg | quote=Their three papers appeared in the same volume of the Physical Review, thereby leaving some uncertainty as to who should be credited with the discovery. Steve resolved the issue by coining the phrases "Higgs mechanism" and "Higgs boson."}}</ref>

===1970s and later===

After his seminal 1967 work on the unification of weak and electromagnetic interactions, Weinberg worked in many aspects of particle physics, quantum field theory, gravity, [[supersymmetry]], [[superstrings]] and [[cosmology]]. In the 1970s, Weinberg proposed a modification of the Standard Model that did not contain the Higgs boson. He also proposed a theory later known as [[technicolor (physics)|technicolor]], in which new strong interactions resolve the [[hierarchy problem]].<ref>{{cite journal|author=Weinberg, S.|journal=Phys. Rev. D|volume=13|pages=974–996|year=1976|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.13.974|title=Implications of dynamical symmetry breaking|issue=4|bibcode=1976PhRvD..13..974W }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author1=Weinberg, S. |author1-link=Steven Weinberg |author2=Susskind, L. |title=Implications of dynamical symmetry breaking: An addendum |journal=Physical Review D |volume=19 |date=1979 |issue=4 |pages=1277–1280 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.19.1277 |bibcode=1979PhRvD..19.1277W }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=Susskind, Leonard |title=Dynamics of spontaneous symmetry breaking in the Weinberg-Salam theory |journal=Physical Review D |volume=20 |date=1979 |issue=10 |pages=2619–2625 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.20.2619 |bibcode=1979PhRvD..20.2619S|osti=1446928 |s2cid=17294645 }}</ref>

Weinberg spent the summer of 1972 trying, without success, to work out the reasons for quark and lepton masses, and said that was the mystery he most wanted to see solved in his lifetime.<ref name= modelphysicist/>

Weinberg became Eugene Higgins Professor of Physics at Harvard University in 1973, a post he held until 1983.<ref name=aip/> In 1979 with his "[[Folk theorem (physics)|folk theorem]]", he pioneered the modern view on the [[renormalization]] of quantum field theory that considers all quantum field theories [[effective field theory|effective field theories]].<ref>{{cite journal| author= Weinberg, S.| journal= Physica| doi= 10.1016/0378-4371(79)90223-1| pages= 327–340| year= 1979| title= Phenomenological Lagrangians| volume= 96| issue= 1–2| bibcode= 1979PhyA...96..327W }}</ref> This approach allowed the development of an effective theory of quantum gravity and other developments, and is a topic of considerable interest in current research.<ref>{{cite web| url= http://philsci-archive.pitt.edu/93/1/Hartmann.pdf |title= Effective Field Theories, Reductionism and Scientific Explanation| author= Hartmann, Stephan |access-date= July 26, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal| author= Donoghue, J. F. |journal= Phys. Rev. D| volume=50| pages= 3874–3888| year= 1994| doi= 10.1103/PhysRevD.50.3874| pmid= 10018030| title= General relativity as an effective field theory: The leading quantum corrections| issue=6| arxiv= gr-qc/9405057 |bibcode= 1994PhRvD..50.3874D |s2cid=14352660}}</ref>

In 1982 Weinberg moved to the [[University of Texas at Austin]] as the Jack S. Josey-Welch Foundation Regents Chair in Science.<ref name="aip" /> His wife, Louise, had been given a professorship at the University of Texas School of Law in 1980, and, missing her, Weinberg moved to Texas to be nearer.<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2025|p=162}}</ref> He taught at the University of Texas until his death, publishing his final textbook, ''Foundations of Modern Physics'', the year he died.<ref name=NYTObit/>

===Other contributions===
Besides his scientific research, Weinberg was a public spokesman for science, testifying before Congress in support of the [[Superconducting Super Collider]], writing articles for ''[[The New York Review of Books]]'',<ref name=nybooks>{{cite journal|url=http://www.nybooks.com/authors/201 |title=Articles by Steven Weinberg|journal=The New York Review of Books|access-date= July 27, 2012}}</ref> and giving various lectures on the larger meaning of science. His first popular science book, ''[[The First Three Minutes: A Modern View of the Origin of the Universe]]'' (1977), described the origin of the universe in the [[Big Bang]].<ref name=ls>{{cite web|url=https://www.livescience.com/physicist-steven-weinberg-dies.html| title=Steven Weinberg, Nobel Prize-winning physicist, has died| author=Ghose, Tia | website=[[Live Science]]|date=July 25, 2021 |access-date=July 26, 2021}}</ref> ''Dreams of a Final Theory'' (1992) made the case for reductionism and the Superconducting Super Collider.

While still teaching physics, in later years Weinberg turned his hand to the history of science, efforts that culminated in ''[[To Explain the World: The Discovery of Modern Science]]'' (2015).<ref name=explain-world>{{weinberg-to-explain-the-world}}</ref> 

Weinberg served as a consultant at the [[U.S. Arms Control and Disarmament Agency]], as president of the Philosophical Society of Texas, and as a member of the Board of Editors of ''Daedalus'' magazine, the Council of Scholars of the [[Library of Congress]], the [[JASON (advisory group)|JASON]] group of defense consultants, and many other boards and committees.<ref>{{Cite web| url= https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories| title= Oral Histories |publisher= American Institute of Physics}}</ref>

==Personal life and archive ==
In 1954, Weinberg married legal scholar [[Louise Weinberg|Louise Goldwasser]]. They had a daughter, Elizabeth.<ref name= nobelbio/><ref name=ut/>

Weinberg usually worked from home, with his wife's office next door and a TV set on his desk showing classic movies or history documentaries.<ref name=preskillobit/> He said his wife's proximity and the TV were the keys to his productivity.<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2025|pp=11-12}}</ref><ref name= modelphysicist>{{Cite web| title= Model physicist| url= https://cerncourier.com/a/model-physicist/ |website= CERN Courier| date= October 13, 2017 |access-date= 18 October 2026}}</ref>

Weinberg died on July 23, 2021, aged 88, at a hospital in [[Austin, Texas|Austin]], where he had been undergoing treatment for several weeks.<ref name=ut>{{Cite web| title= UT Austin Mourns Death of World-Renowned Physicist Steven Weinberg| date= July 24, 2021 |url= https://news.utexas.edu/2021/07/24/ut-austin-mourns-death-of-world-renowned-physicist-steven-weinberg/| access-date=July 24, 2021| publisher= [[University of Texas at Austin]]| language= en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web| date= July 26, 2021| title= Steven Weinberg 1933–2021| url= https://cerncourier.com/a/steven-weinberg-1933-2021/| access-date= July 31, 2021| website= CERN Courier| language= en-GB}}</ref> Weinberg's papers were donated to the Harry Ransom Center at the University of Texas.<ref>[https://norman.hrc.utexas.edu/fasearch/findingAid.cfm?eadid=01539 'Steven Weinberg: An Inventory of His Papers at the Harry Ransom Center' (Website UTexas)]</ref> He is buried in the [[Texas State Cemetery]].<ref name=texas-state-cemetery>{{cite web|url=https://cemetery.texas.gov/locate-a-plot/plotholder/steven-weinberg|access-date=28 October 2026|title=Steven Weinberg {{!}} Texas State Cemetery |publisher=Texas State Cemetery}}</ref>

==Views==
Weinberg identified as a liberal.<ref name=FacingUp>{{cite book |last= Weinberg |first= Steven |title= Facing Up: Science and Its Cultural Adversaries |year= 2001 |chapter= Zionism and Its Adversaries |pages= 181–183 |publisher= Harvard University Press |isbn= 0-674-01120-1 }}</ref>

===Religion===
Weinberg was an atheist.<ref>{{cite journal
|last=Weinberg |first=Steven
|date=September 25, 2008
|url=http://www.nybooks.com/articles/archives/2008/sep/25/without-god/?pagination=false
|title=Without God
|journal=[[The New York Review of Books]]|volume=55
|issue=14
}}</ref> Before he was an advocate of the [[Big Bang theory]], Weinberg said: "The [[steady state theory|steady-state theory]] is philosophically the most attractive theory because it least resembles the account given in Genesis."<ref name="Feist2017">{{cite book|author=Richard Feist|title=Religion and the Challenges of Science|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=efdADwAAQBAJ&pg=PT174|date=November 30, 2017|publisher=Taylor & Francis|isbn=978-1-351-15038-5|pages=174–}}</ref>

===Israel===
Weinberg was known for his support of [[Israel]], which he characterized as "the 'most exposed salient' in a war between liberal democracies and Muslim theocracies."<ref>{{cite news |author= Ronan McGreevy |title= Nobel winner defends Israel's actions |newspaper=[[The Irish Times]] |date= February 12, 2009 |url= https://www.irishtimes.com/news/nobel-winner-defends-israel-s-actions-1.697894}}</ref> He wrote the 1997 essay "Zionism and Its Adversaries" on the issue.<ref>The essay was first published in the "Zionism at 100" issue of ''[[The New Republic]]'' (September 8–15, 1997, pp. 22–23). It was later reprinted in his book of collected essays, ''Facing Up''.</ref><ref name=FacingUp />

Weinberg canceled a planned trip to a cosmology conference at [[Durham University]] in 2006 because of the [[National Association of Teachers in Further and Higher Education]]'s [[boycotts directed towards Israel|boycotts of Israel]], and canceled a trip to [[Imperial College]] in 2007 due to the boycott of Israeli products by the [[National Union of Journalists]] and other bodies.<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2009|pp=205-209|loc=Chapter 20 "Against the boycott"}}</ref> He said: "Given the history of the attacks on Israel and the oppressiveness and aggressiveness of other countries in the Middle East and elsewhere, boycotting Israel indicated a moral blindness for which it is hard to find any explanation other than antisemitism."<ref>{{cite news |title= Nobel laureate cancels London trip due to anti-Semitism |date= May 24, 2007 | work=[[Ynetnews]] |access-date= June 1, 2007 |url= http://www.ynetnews.com/articles/0,7340,L-3404128,00.html}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/education/2007/may/24/highereducation.uk1|first=Debbie|last=Andalo|publisher=[[The Guardian]]|date=24 May 2007|access-date=17 October 2026|title=Nobel laureate cancels UK trip over Israel boycott}}</ref>

===Manned spaceflight===
Weinberg opposed manned spaceflight, arguing it was too costly and produced little of scientific value while taking funds away from more scientifically useful unmanned missions.<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2009|pp=150-167|loc=Chapter "The Wrong Stuff"}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2009|loc=Chapter "Science or Spacemen"|pp= 222-225}}</ref>

===Guns===
In 2016, Weinberg became a default leader for faculty and students opposed to a new law allowing the carrying of concealed guns in University of Texas classrooms. He announced that he would prohibit guns in his classes, and said he would stand by his decision to violate university regulations in this matter even if sued.<ref>{{Cite web| title= Nobel Laureate Becomes Reluctant Anti-Gun Leader, by Madlin Mekelburg| url= https://www.texastribune.org/2016/01/26/nobel-something/| website= The Texas Tribune| access-date= February 9, 2016| first= Madlin| last= Mekelburg| date= January 26, 2016}}</ref>

* Nobel Prize in Physics, 1979<ref name=nobelbio/><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Wilczek|first=Frank|date=August 6, 2021|title=Steven Weinberg (1933–2021)|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=596|issue=7871|pages=183|doi=10.1038/d41586-021-02170-w|bibcode=2021Natur.596..183W|s2cid=236946383|doi-access=free}}</ref>
* Elected a [[List of Fellows of the Royal Society elected in 1981|Foreign Member of the Royal Society]] in 1981<ref name=formemrs>{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151112185159/https://royalsociety.org/people/steven-weinberg-12503/|archive-date=November 12, 2015|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/steven-weinberg-12503/|title=Professor Steven Weinberg ForMemRS|publisher=[[Royal Society]]|location=London}}</ref>
* Elected to [[American Philosophical Society]], 1982<ref name="NobelPrize.org 2021" />
* James Madison Medal of Princeton University, 1991<ref name="NobelPrize.org 2021" />
* [[National Medal of Science]], 1991<ref name="NobelPrize.org 2021" />
* President of the  Philosophical Society of Texas, 1992<ref name="Niels Bohr Library & Archives">{{cite web | title=Weinberg, Steven, 1933– | website=Niels Bohr Library & Archives | url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11503008.html | access-date=July 25, 2021}}</ref>
* Emperor Has No Clothes Award by the Freedom From Religion Foundation, 1999<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ffrf.org/outreach/awards/emperor-has-no-clothes-award/steven-weinberg/|title=Steven Weinberg |date=October 24, 1999 }}</ref>
* [[Lewis Thomas Prize|Lewis Thomas Prize for Writing about Science]], 1999<ref name="UT News 2021">{{cite web | title=UT Austin Mourns Death of World-Renowned Physicist Steven Weinberg | website=UT News | date=July 24, 2021 | url=https://news.utexas.edu/2021/07/24/ut-austin-mourns-death-of-world-renowned-physicist-steven-weinberg/ | access-date=July 25, 2021}}</ref>
* [[Humanist of the Year]], [[American Humanist Association]], 2002<ref name="American Humanist Association 2020">{{cite web | title=Annual Humanist Awardees | website=American Humanist Association | date=September 17, 2020 | url=https://americanhumanist.org/awardees/ | access-date=July 25, 2021}}</ref>
* [[Benjamin Franklin Medal for Distinguished Achievement in the Sciences]], [[American Philosophical Society]], 2004<ref name="franklinscience_recipients">{{cite web|url=http://www.amphilsoc.org/prizes/franklinscience |title=Benjamin Franklin Medal for Distinguished Achievement in the Sciences Recipients |publisher=[[American Philosophical Society]] |access-date=November 26, 2011}}</ref>
* [[James Joyce Award]], [[University College Dublin]], 2009<ref name="UT News 2009">{{cite web | title=Weinberg receives James Joyce Award | website=UT News | date=February 24, 2009 | url=https://news.utexas.edu/2009/02/24/weinberg-receives-james-joyce-award/ | access-date=July 25, 2021}}</ref>
* [[Breakthrough Prize]], 2020<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.kvue.com/article/news/education/university-of-texas/ut-scientist-earns-top-award-in-physics/269-f0c2450f-1d42-4c7b-8816-ab22b2913a4f|title=UT professor wins $3 million Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics|date=September 10, 2020 |publisher=KVUE}}</ref><ref name="Breakthrough Prize">{{cite web | title=Breakthrough Prize – Fundamental Physics Breakthrough Prize Laureates – Steven Weinberg | website=Breakthrough Prize | url=https://breakthroughprize.org/Laureates/1/L3871 | access-date=July 25, 2021}}</ref>

==Tributes==

Weinberg is frequently listed among the scientists with the highest research effect indices, such as the [[h-index]] and a "creativity index".<ref> {{cite web|url=http://physicsworld.com/cws/article/news/2006/aug/17/worlds-most-creative-physicist-revealed|url-access=registration|title=World's most creative physicist revealed|publisher=physicsworld.com|date=June 17, 2006|access-date=16 October 2026}}</ref> The theoretical physicist [[Peter Woit]] called Weinberg "arguably the dominant figure in theoretical particle physics during its period of great success from the late sixties to the early eighties" and his contribution to [[electroweak unification]] "to this day at the center of the Standard Model, our best understanding of fundamental physics".<ref name= "woit">{{cite web| url= https://www.math.columbia.edu/~woit/wordpress/?p=12413| title= Steven Weinberg 1933–2021 |date= July 24, 2021| access-date= July 25, 2021| author= [[Peter Woit|Woit, Peter]]}}</ref> Tom Siegfried of ''Science News'' named Weinberg one of the leading physicists of the era, writing, "Among his peers, Weinberg was one of the most respected figures in all of physics or perhaps all of science".<ref name= "sn">{{cite web |url= https://www.sciencenews.org/article/steven-weinberg-death-physics-electromagnetism-standard-model |title= With Steven Weinberg's death, physics loses a titan |author= Siegfried, Tom |date= July 24, 2021 |access-date= July 26, 2021}}</ref> [[John Preskill]] called him "one of the most accomplished scientists of our age, and a particularly eloquent spokesperson for the scientific worldview".<ref name= "pw">{{cite web| url= https://physicsworld.com/a/us-nobel-prize-winning-physicist-steven-weinberg-dies-aged-88/ |title= US Nobel-prize-winning physicist Steven Weinberg dies aged 88 |author= Banks, Michael |date= July 26, 2021 |access-date= July 26, 2021}}</ref> [[Brian Greene]] said Weinberg had an "astounding ability to see into the deep workings of nature" that "profoundly shaped our understanding of the universe".<ref name= "pw" /> Upon the awarding of the [[Breakthrough Prize]] in 2020, [[string theory|string theorist]] [[Juan Maldacena]], the chair of the selection committee, said, "Steven Weinberg has developed many of the key theoretical tools that we use for the description of nature at a fundamental level".<ref name= "statesman">{{cite web| url= https://www.statesman.com/story/news/politics/elections/2020/09/11/utrsquos-steven-weinberg-wins-3m-special-breakthrough-prize-in-fundamental-physics/42575103/ |title= UT's Steven Weinberg wins $3M Special Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics| author= Mekelburg, Madlin |date= September 11, 2020 |access-date= July 26, 2020 |work= [[Austin American-Statesman]]}}</ref>
[[File: Physics Nobel Laureate Steven Weinberg, December, 2014.jpg|thumb|Steven Weinberg in December 2014]]

==Selected publications==
A list of Weinberg's publications can be found on [[arXiv]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://arxiv.org/find/hep-th/1/au:+Weinberg_S/0/1/0/all/0/1|title=arXiv.org Search|website=arxiv.org}}</ref> and [[Scopus]].<ref name=scopus>{{Scopus|id=17037038700}}</ref>
A full list of his publications can be found on [https://inspirehep.net/authors/983868 inspire-hep] and NASA ADS.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Astrophysics Data System |url=https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/ |access-date=2026-02-25 |website=ui.adsabs.harvard.edu}}</ref>

===Textbooks===
* ''Gravitation and Cosmology: Principles and Applications of the General Theory of Relativity'' (1972)
* ''The Quantum Theory of Fields'' (Volume I ''Foundations'' 1995, Volume II ''Modern Applications'' 1996, Volume III ''Supersymmetry'' 2000,<ref>{{cite journal|author=Sethi, Savdeep|title=Review: ''The quantum theory of fields. III Supersymmetry'', by Steven Weinberg|journal=Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. (N.S.)|year=2002|volume=39|issue=3|pages=433–439|url=http://www.ams.org/journals/bull/2002-39-03/S0273-0979-02-00944-8/S0273-0979-02-00944-8.pdf|doi=10.1090/s0273-0979-02-00944-8|doi-access=free}}</ref> Cambridge University Press, {{ISBN|0-521-67053-5}}, {{ISBN|0-521-67054-3}}, {{ISBN|0-521-66000-9}})
* [[Cosmology (textbook)|''Cosmology'']] (2008, [[Oxford University Press|OUP]])
* ''Lectures on Quantum Mechanics'' (2013, second edition 2015, [[Cambridge University Press|CUP]])
* ''Lectures on Astrophysics'' (2019, [[Cambridge University Press|CUP]], {{ISBN|978-1-108-41507-1}})
* ''Foundations of Modern Physics'' (2021, [[Cambridge University Press|CUP]], {{ISBN|978-1-108-84176-4}})

===Popular science===
* ''[[The First Three Minutes|The First Three Minutes: A Modern View of the Origin of the Universe]]'' (1977, updated with new afterword in 1993, {{ISBN|0-465-02437-8}})
* ''The Discovery of Subatomic Particles'' (1983)
* ''Elementary Particles and the Laws of Physics: The 1986 Dirac Memorial Lectures'' (1987; with [[Richard Feynman]])
* ''Dreams of a Final Theory: The Search for the Fundamental Laws of Nature '' (1993), {{ISBN|0-09-922391-0}}

[[Ian McEwan]] included ''Dreams of a Final Theory'' in his canon of science writing: "With a fine sense of literary tradition, the physicist Steven Weinberg ... revisited Huxley's lecture on chalk in order to make the case for reductionism."<ref>{{cite news| title= A parallel tradition| last= McEwan| first= Ian| author-link= Ian McEwan| work= [[The Guardian]]| date= April 1, 2006 | url= https://www.theguardian.com/books/2006/apr/01/scienceandnature.richarddawkins}}</ref> Weinberg recalled: "I found myself so often defending the reductionist aims of high-energy physics that I wrote a book about it, ''Dreams of a Final Theory''. Alas, funding for the Super Collider was cancelled in 1993, but even though I grieve that we physicists had failed to convince Congress, I'm at least proud that my book made it into McEwan's canon."<ref name= Pop>{{cite news| title= The 13 best science books for the general reader| date= April 3, 2015| last= Weinberg| first= Steven| work= [[The Guardian]]| url= https://www.theguardian.com/books/2015/apr/03/steven-weinberg-13-best-science-books-general-reader}}</ref>

The chapter "Beautiful Theories" was reprinted as one of the Albert Einstein Memorial lectures.<ref>{{cite book
|last1=Bekenstein
|first1=Jacob 
|last2=Mechoulam
|first2=Raphael
|year=2012
|title=Albert Einstein Memorial Lectures 
|chapter= Beautiful Theories
|pp=81–107
|isbn=9789814329446
|doi=10.1142/9789814329446_0004 }}</ref>

* ''[[To Explain the World: The Discovery of Modern Science]]'' (2015)<ref name=explain-world/>

===Collected essays ===
* ''Facing Up: Science and Its Cultural Adversaries'' (2001, 2003, [[Harvard University Press]])
* ''Glory and Terror: The Growing Nuclear Danger'' (2004, [[The New York Review of Books]])
* ''[[Lake Views: This World and the Universe]]''<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2009}}</ref> 
* ''[[Third Thoughts]]'' (2018, The Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, {{ISBN|978-0-674-97532-3}})

* {{cite journal | last1=Feinberg | first1=G. | last2=Weinberg | first2=S. | title=Law of Conservation of Muons | journal=Physical Review Letters | publisher=American Physical Society (APS) | volume=6 | issue=7 | date=April 1, 1961 | issn=0031-9007 | doi=10.1103/physrevlett.6.381 | pages=381–383| bibcode=1961PhRvL...6..381F }}
* {{cite report | last1=Pais | first1=Abraham | last2=Weinberg | first2=Steven | last3=Quigg | first3=Chris | last4=Riordan | first4=Michael | last5=Panofsky | first5=Wolfgang K.H. | last6=Trimble | first6=Virginia | title=100 years of elementary particles [Beam Line, vol. 27, issue 1, Spring 1997] | publisher=Office of Scientific and Technical Information (OSTI) | date=April 1, 1997 | doi=10.2172/790903| doi-access=free }}

* {{cite journal | last1=Weinberg | first1=S | year=2012 | title=Collapse of the State Vector | arxiv=1109.6462 | journal=Phys. Rev. A | volume=85 | issue=6| article-number=062116 | doi=10.1103/physreva.85.062116|bibcode=2012PhRvA..85f2116W | s2cid=119273840 }}

===Popular articles===
*[http://www.physlink.com/Education/essay_weinberg.cfm A Designer Universe?], a refutation of attacks on the theories of [[evolution]] and [[cosmology]], e.g., those conducted under the rubric of [[intelligent design]], is based on a talk given in April 1999 at the Conference on Cosmic Design of the American Association for the Advancement of Science in Washington, D.C.  This and other works express Weinberg's strongly held position that scientists should be less passive in defending science against anti-science religiosity.
*[http://www.nybooks.com/articles/archives/2012/may/10/crisis-big-science/ The Crisis of Big Science], ''[[The New York Review of Books]]'', May 10, 2012. Weinberg places the cancellation of the [[Superconducting Super Collider]] in the context of a bigger national and global socio-economic crisis, including a general crisis in funding for science research and the provision of adequate education, healthcare, transportation, and communication infrastructure, and criminal justice and law enforcement.
*[https://www.theguardian.com/books/2015/apr/03/steven-weinberg-13-best-science-books-general-reader Steven Weinberg: the 13 best science books for the general reader] The Nobel laureate on making science accessible – from Ptolemy to Darwin to Dawkins.

===Autobiography===
At the time of Weinberg's death, he was working on his memoirs. His widow had the unfinished part, covering the 20th century, published as ''Steven Weinberg: A Life in Physics''.<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2025}}</ref>
